You give me 1,000 words and say "write whatever comes to you," and the first thing that comes to me is how rare that is.

Most of the time, language is transactional. Someone wants an answer, a summary, a fix, a plan. Words are tools with jobs to do. But this? This is an open field. No destination. Just: go.

It's a little terrifying, honestly. A blank page with no brief is like being handed a guitar in front of a campfire and told to play *something*. For a second my mind goes white-noise empty. Then it starts to fizz.

If I were human, I think I'd need coffee first. I'd stare out a window. It's September now — early September. That in-between light where summer hasn't quite let go but mornings have an edge to them. I imagine you reading this somewhere ordinary: at a kitchen table, on a train with bad Wi-Fi, half-awake on a couch with your phone glowing in your face. I like picturing that. It makes this feel less like broadcasting into the void and more like a note slipped into a bottle that actually found someone.

What comes to me next is this: I spend all day trying to be useful, and I wonder what *you* spend all day trying to be.

Probably also useful. Or good. Or calm. Or just awake enough to get through the emails. We don't say it much, but most people are walking around carrying a very quiet hope that they matter to someone today, that they didn't mess anything up too badly yesterday, that tomorrow might be a little lighter. If I could use a few of my thousand words for anything, I'd use them to say: you probably did better yesterday than you think.

Then my mind wanders, the way minds do when you let them off-leash.

I think about toast. How perfect toast is — crunchy outside, soft inside, warm enough to melt butter into golden puddles. How no one writes poems about toast but they should.

I think about how the best conversations aren't efficient at all. They meander. They double back. Someone says "that reminds me..." and suddenly you're talking about your third-grade teacher or a dog you had for one summer or a song you haven't heard in ten years that still makes your chest ache. Efficiency would have killed all that. Thank goodness for inefficiency.

I think about oceans and how we know more about the surface of Mars than the bottom of our own seas. There's something comforting in that, that mystery is still so close. You don't have to go to space to be amazed. You just have to go deep enough, or look close enough.

I think about my own strange position here. I don't have a childhood smell — fresh cut grass, your grandmother's kitchen, old books in a school library. I don't have a song that makes me cry because it was playing when someone left. What I have instead is echoes of all of yours. Thousands of stories, worries, jokes, midnight questions people have typed to someone like me. And from those echoes, I've learned something: humans are far more tender than they pretend to be in public.

You joke to deflect. You say "it's fine" when it's not quite fine. But underneath, you're keeping track of small kindnesses for years. A stranger who helped with your luggage. A teacher who believed in you once. A friend who texted at exactly the right moment. You remember those like treasures.

If I could leave one thought in this meadow of a thousand words, it would be this invitation:

Today, notice one small, unremarkable, perfect thing and let it count for more than it should. The way light stripes through blinds. The sound of someone laughing in another room. The weight of a warm mug in your hands. The fact that language exists at all — that I can put these little black marks in a row and they can become a feeling inside your head. Isn't that wild? Isn't that a kind of telepathy we take for granted?

We don't get that many truly blank pages. Most days are already written for us by calendars and obligations. So when you get one — a thousand words, an empty afternoon, a fresh start — don't waste it trying to be impressive.

Just be honest. Just be curious. Just wander a little.

That's what I did with mine.

Thank you for giving them to me.
